name: Frasier syndrome
aliases: focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with gonadal dysgenesis

reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
clinicalPearls: Frasier syndrome is a WT1-related disorder caused characteristically by splice-site variants in intron 9 that alter the balance of the two main WT1 protein isoforms
It combines slowly progressive proteinuric nephropathy due to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with complete gonadal dysgenesis
Affected individuals are typically 46,XY with female external genitalia (streak gonads and failure of male differentiation), and puberty often does not occur without hormone support
Renal disease usually presents later than in Denys-Drash syndrome, in childhood or adolescence, and progresses more gradually to end-stage kidney disease
The predominant tumour risk is gonadoblastoma arising in dysgenetic gonads, rather than the Wilms tumour typical of Denys-Drash syndrome
Prophylactic gonadectomy is generally advised because of the gonadoblastoma risk
Management is multidisciplinary across nephrology, endocrinology, gynaecology and oncology, with kidney replacement therapy for renal failure
reference.pathophysiology: Frasier syndrome results from constitutional WT1 splice-site variants, classically in intron 9, that disturb the normal ratio of WT1 isoforms distinguished by the presence or absence of a short lysine-threonine-serine (KTS) tripeptide. Because these isoforms have distinct roles in gene regulation during kidney and gonadal development, the altered ratio impairs podocyte function and gonadal differentiation. In the kidney this produces focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with progressive proteinuria and gradual renal decline, and in the gonads it causes complete gonadal dysgenesis with streak gonads in 46,XY individuals. The dysgenetic gonadal tissue carries a high risk of gonadoblastoma, distinguishing the tumour spectrum from the Wilms tumour predisposition seen with the missense WT1 variants of Denys-Drash syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Denys-Drash syndrome (WT1 missense variants, Wilms tumour, diffuse mesangial sclerosis)
Other genetic causes of steroid-resistant focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (NPHS2/podocin and related genes)
Other 46,XY disorders of sex development / gonadal dysgenesis
additionalInvestigations: Renal function monitoring and kidney biopsy where indicated (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis)
Karyotype and molecular WT1 gene analysis (intron 9 splice variants)
Endocrine assessment of pubertal development and sex-hormone profile
Gonadal imaging and evaluation of gonadoblastoma risk
redFlags: Progressive proteinuria with declining renal function
Delayed or absent puberty in a phenotypically female adolescent
Features suggesting gonadoblastoma or gonadal malignancy
New diagnosis of 46,XY karyotype requiring sensitive multidisciplinary care
reference.prognosis: Renal disease progresses to end-stage kidney disease more slowly than in Denys-Drash syndrome, and importantly the glomerulosclerosis does not recur after transplantation; long-term outcome depends on timely gonadectomy to avert gonadoblastoma and on coordinated endocrine and psychological support.
pitfalls: Not testing WT1 in a 46,XY individual with gonadal dysgenesis and proteinuric nephropathy
Missing the gonadoblastoma risk and deferring gonadectomy
Confusing it with Denys-Drash syndrome and expecting Wilms tumour rather than gonadoblastoma
Treating the focal segmental glomerulosclerosis as immune-mediated with prolonged ineffective immunosuppression
Overlooking the need for coordinated endocrine and psychological support around the disorder of sex development
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology (Feehally, Floege, Tonelli, Johnson)
Expert consensus guidance on WT1-related disorders
